title: Breadth-First Search (BFS) Traversal
teaching_goal: Understand BFS core concepts, queue mechanism, trace execution, and standard code implementation.

scenes.title: What is Breadth-First Search?
scenes.subtitle: Breadth-First Search is a core traversal algorithm that explores graph nodes layer by layer.

visual_data.definition: An algorithm for searching a tree or graph data structure. It starts at the root node and explores all neighboring nodes at the present depth level before moving to nodes at the next depth level.
features: Explores layer by layer (level order layout)
Uses a FIFO Queue to track frontier nodes
Guarantees shortest path on unweighted graphs
visual_data.summary: BFS is optimal for finding shortest paths in unweighted networks.

scenes.title: How Queue Tracks the Frontier
scenes.subtitle: BFS uses a Queue. Let's see how nodes are pushed and popped during execution.

operations.explanation: We start by enqueuing the start node A.
Dequeue node A to visit it, preparing to examine its neighbors.
Enqueue neighbor C. Now the queue has B and C.

scenes.title: BFS Level-Order Tree Traversal
scenes.subtitle: Let's trace the traversal order of a simple binary tree.

steps.explanation: Visit root node A, and add neighbors B and C to queue.
Visit node B, and add its neighbors D and E to the queue.
Visit node C, it has no unvisited neighbors.
Visit leaf node E. The queue is now empty.

scenes.title: BFS Summary & Exam Guide
scenes.subtitle: To summarize, BFS is a queue-based traversal optimized for finding the shortest path.

visual_data.title: BFS Key Takeaways
key_points: Time Complexity: O(V + E) where V is vertices, E is edges
Space Complexity: O(V) to store queue and visited set
Applicability: Best for unweighted shortest path and level-order print
visual_data.exam_focus: In exams, remember that BFS uses a queue, while DFS uses a stack. Don't mix them up!
